title: From Honor to Ridicule and Pain
overview: Job describes how far he has fallen: mocked by society's lowest outcasts, wracked by illness, and crying out to a God who seems silent and hostile.

parts.label: Mocked by outcasts (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: In the previous chapter Job remembered being honored by everyone; now he is laughed at by young men from families driven out of the villages, who lived in caves and ate bitter desert plants. His harsh words about them show how deeply he feels the loss of his standing, judged by the social rankings of his own world.

parts.label: Songs, spit and attacks (vv. 9-15)
parts.note: Job says God has loosened a cord, an image that may picture his strength gone slack like an unstrung bow, though the Hebrew is unclear. With nothing holding them back, these men make up mocking songs, spit at him and pour in like soldiers through a broken city wall; Christians later saw in this mockery an echo of how Jesus was treated.

parts.label: Pain that never rests (vv. 16-19)
parts.note: Job's illness torments him most at night, and he feels God gripping him as tightly as the collar of a garment, though scholars are unsure of the exact sense of verse 18. Being thrown into mud and ashes likely recalls Job sitting in ashes as a mourner when his suffering began.

parts.label: Crying to a silent God (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: Job stands and pleads with God the way someone would before a king, but God only stares, then seems to attack him and toss him about like something caught in a storm. He now expects nothing but death, the place where every living thing ends up.

parts.label: Kindness repaid with darkness (vv. 24-31)
parts.note: Job argues that anyone in ruin may cry for help, especially since he once wept for the poor, yet when he hoped for good, evil came; verse 24 is hard to translate and is read in several ways. His blackened, peeling skin, his kinship with jackals and lonely desert birds (translations differ between owls and ostriches), and his music turned to wailing all picture complete grief.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Job's bold accusations against God here are honest lament that God accepts, since God later says Job spoke rightly, or words that go too far, since Job later takes back what he said.
think: Should being good to others protect a person from disaster, and if it doesn't, what do you make of that?
